name: TongaLang
shortDescription: A beginner-focused interpreted programming language with Tonga-derived keywords, guided error recovery and an installable desktop IDE.

problem: Beginner programmers may need to learn programming concepts and interpret unfamiliar English syntax at the same time, adding linguistic and cognitive load.
solution: TongaLang combines Tonga-derived vocabulary with a small interpreted language and a guided desktop workspace. Learners see concepts in context, receive a plain-language recovery step when code is wrong, and stay in control of every suggested edit. Version 0.2.0 can be installed directly on Windows, while documented source and native bundle paths support Linux. It remains an educational language rather than a replacement for mainstream production tools.
contributions: Researched minimal languages and interpreter construction, then mapped core programming concepts into Tonga-derived vocabulary through linguistic research and native-speaker consultation.
Built the lexer, parser, abstract syntax tree, interpreter, runtime environment and native functions before separating the language engine from its Tkinter IDE.
Designed a pure diagnostics model with stable codes, exact source spans, bilingual explanations and guarded edits that never execute or silently rewrite learner code.
Added debounced live analysis and a collapsible Problems workflow with precise highlighting, Go to Code, Copy Details and undoable Apply Fix actions.
Reworked graphical input around one thread-safe shared dock so bala() pauses only the interpreter, keeps the interface responsive and echoes submitted values into Output.
Created the TongaLang visual identity and applied it consistently to the IDE window, executable, desktop shortcut and setup experience.
Built a reproducible Windows installer that installs per user, includes 17 examples and supports clean uninstallation without requiring administrator access.
Documented Linux source installation and native bundle creation, then published the checksum-verified v0.2.0 release with privacy-reviewed product evidence.

challenges.title: Helpful fixes without unsafe guessing
challenges.description: The IDE needed broad recovery advice while editing only deterministic mistakes. Suggested edits therefore carry the expected original text, reject stale source and leave ambiguous choices to the learner.

challenges.title: Input without freezing the IDE
challenges.description: bala() must pause execution, not navigation or scrolling. A worker-thread input provider and single-use queue handoff keep Tkinter responsive and prevent repeated submissions.

challenges.title: One dock across changing views
challenges.description: Problems and Program Input share state, expansion and sash size while Editor and Output change underneath them. Runtime failures, successful runs, pending input and manual inspection each require a distinct transition.

challenges.title: Growing without regressions
challenges.description: Diagnostics, tokens, grammar, runtime behaviour, highlighting and existing programs affect one another, so changes are protected by error-contract, adversarial and GUI integration tests.

challenges.title: Packaging a complete learning environment
challenges.description: The desktop release needed more than a frozen executable. The build now carries the logo, runtime assets and examples into a per-user installer, documents reproducible builds and publishes a checksum for independent verification.

Add keyword and native-function autocomplete with short contextual help
Add a variable inspector and simple step-through execution

name: SmartWater Zambia
shortDescription: IoT water telemetry and community incident reporting, built as one platform across an ESP32 sensor, an operator dashboard and a native Android app.

problem: Zambian utilities keep instrumentation at treatment works and district meters but very little between the district meter and the customer, so leaks and shortages surface as phone calls and reconciled bills days later. Residents have no dependable signal for how much water is actually in a shared tank, and incident reports arrive without consistent categories, locations or a record of what was checked.
solution: SmartWater Zambia puts three layers on one data contract: an ESP32 ultrasonic sensor posts calibrated readings to an authenticated API, an operator dashboard tracks levels, alerts and community reports in real time, and a native Android app gives residents the same picture plus a route onto the incident map.
contributions: Built the Express API behind the platform: JWT role authentication plus per-device API keys, IoT ingestion, threshold alerting, heartbeat and offline detection, and a Server-Sent Events hub with a polling fallback.

Built the React administration dashboard: live tank cards, Chart.js history, a Leaflet incident map, community report case management and analytics, the alerts centre, the hardware simulator and the installation and calibration screens.
Built the native Android customer app in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose: live level gauges, saved locations, map-based report submission, notifications and Google sign-in.

Wired the physical demo: one ESP32 ultrasonic sensor on a real tank streaming into the same API the dashboard and app read, with the remaining tanks simulated so the operator view could be shown at realistic scale.
features: Device-authenticated IoT ingestion with raw payload retention
Calibrated depth, tank geometry and volume estimation
Live tank levels over Server-Sent Events
Community incident reports with photos and coordinates
Report case lifecycle with full status history
Report intelligence with response and category analysis
Installation and calibration records per tank
Sensor fault logging without fabricated readings
Native Android app with live gauges and notifications
Role-based access for administrators, customers and technicians

challenges.title: Telemetry that does not invent data
challenges.description: A sensor timeout, a bad reading and a genuinely empty tank look similar from a distance. The platform records sensor faults as their own event, flags stale readings instead of repeating the last value, and labels every simulated tank so an operator can separate what was measured from what was seeded.

challenges.title: One contract, three clients
challenges.description: Firmware, dashboard and Android app had to agree on distance, depth, level and volume while the device side stayed minimal. Calibration and geometry live on the server, so the ESP32 posts centimetres and both clients read the same derived state over REST and SSE.

challenges.title: A 48-hour build that still behaved like a system
challenges.description: The stack ran on SQLite locally and Supabase PostgreSQL in deployment, so every schema change had to survive both; realtime used SSE with a polling fallback, because a dropped stream must not look like a tank that stopped changing.

plannedFeatures: Field calibration of the sensor against manual measurements
SMS and USSD channels for residents without smartphones
Integration with utility billing and district-metering systems

audience.why: Zambia’s eleven commercial utilities and six private schemes hold instrumentation at treatment works and district meters, and very little between that and the customer. This targets exactly that gap: storage visibility plus a queue of citizen-reported incidents carrying a location and a photo.

Campuses, hospitals, boarding houses, hotels, mines and commercial farms all store water in tanks someone has to walk to and read. A sensor and a dashboard replace that trip with a timestamped number and an alert.
Buildings with per-block storage can see level and consumption per tank, and route tenant complaints into one case history instead of scattered phone calls.
Programmes need verifiable reporting on what was installed, what was measured and what was fixed. The installation, calibration and case-history records exist to produce that trail.
The people at the end of the pipe are beneficiaries rather than buyers: see the level in your own tank, report a burst pipe with a pin and a photo, and follow the case to resolution.

marketPoints: Sector non-revenue water reached 57% in 2023 against a regulator benchmark of under 20% for good performance — no Zambian utility is close.
The water that is billed costs about K12.61 per unit to deliver and sells for an average of K7.90, and all eleven utilities sit below 100% cost coverage by collection.
The national strategy put revenue lost to non-revenue water at ZMW 998.6 million on a 2020 baseline, against a benchmark loss of ZMW 474.5 million.

Lusaka produced roughly 350,000 m³/day against 480,000 m³/day of demand, dropping to about 265,000 during the 2025 drought — when supply is intermittent, tank-level certainty stops being a convenience.

Roughly 8.36 million people live inside commercial-utility service areas, and coverage fractions fell as population grew faster than connections. Utilities are running to stand still without better information at the edge.
productionPath: Field calibration: run the recorded empty/full reference protocol against a physical tank and log the error, because an uncalibrated ultrasonic reading is a guess with a timestamp.
Hardware hardening: enclosure, power, sensor dead zones and per-device provisioning at scale.
Security review before exposure: server-side enforcement instead of relying on row-level security alone, authenticated realtime streams and credential rotation.
Integration with what utilities already run — billing systems and district metering — so a reading becomes revenue or a work order rather than another dashboard.
Channels that match the user: SMS and USSD paths for residents without smartphones, alongside the Android app.
A pilot with one institution or one utility zone, with a baseline, a measured outcome and an exit decision.
limitations: One physical ESP32 sensor was connected at the hackathon and monitored a real tank (TANK_001, the tank used in the live demo). Additional tanks and stations were simulated so the operator view could be shown at realistic scale, and every simulated record is labelled as such in the interface.
Report-intelligence figures in these captures come from a seeded demo cohort, not a live utility dataset.
Calibration against manual measurements, production deployment and utility integration are still to be done.
evidence: Repository audited on 1 November 2026 at commit 3143c77: ESP32 firmware, the Express and Supabase API, the React/Vite dashboard and the Kotlin/Jetpack Compose Android app are all present alongside backend and web test suites. The team placed in the top six at the GreenCode Hackathon Zambia Edition.

name: SubTrack BH
shortDescription: A local-first Android workspace for operating a boarding-house internet subscription service.
coverAlt: SubTrack BH internet subscription manager logo
problem: Subscriber names, packages, payments, expiry dates, balances and reconnections become unreliable when managed through memory, messages or separate records.
solution: SubTrack BH runs Leo’s live Starlink service end to end for 37 paying subscribers: a subscriber signs up, pays, and the platform verifies the payment and provisions or suspends network access on the router automatically. Room is the local source of truth, with Firebase services for accounts and messaging.
contributions: Modelled subscribers, rooms, plans, devices, payments, expenses, reminders and subscription windows.
Separated administration, subscriber, core, backend and Firebase concerns across project modules.
Added accounting, reconciliation, reporting, backup and PDF utilities.
Wired payment verification to router automation, so a confirmed subscription maps to real MikroTik bandwidth limits without manual work.
Designed the product around the actual workflow of operating the service.
features: Separate admin and subscriber Android apps
Room as the admin app's local source of truth
Subscriber, room, plan and device records
Accounting, reports, backups and PDF utilities
Firebase authentication, Firestore, Storage and messaging
Salted PIN security and failed-attempt lockout
Automatic MikroTik access provisioning and suspension

name: CBU-FIND
shortDescription: A completed cross-platform lost-and-found system that moves campus recovery from scattered group updates into a searchable, verified workflow.
repositoryLabel: Unified Android, web and Worker source
coverAlt: Responsive CBU Find report feed populated with meaningful lost and found items and matched report states
updateSummary: Completed and verified the shared Android/web workflow with meaningful reports, deterministic claim acceptance, private handover conversations, message controls, report resolution, moderation and resilient error states.

media.caption: The responsive web feed exposes the same searchable lost-and-found records as Android, including clear lost, found, active and matched states.

problem: Lost-property information shared through chats, noticeboards and word of mouth is fragmented, difficult to search and easy to miss.
solution: CBU-FIND gives Android and web users one Firebase-backed campus record for publishing reports, verifying ownership claims, opening private handover chats only after acceptance, and closing the recovery loop when an item is returned.
contributions: Designed and built the native Android experience with Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, Material 3 and adaptive light/dark themes.
Built the responsive Vinext/React web client against the same authentication, report, claim, conversation and moderation contracts.
Implemented a trusted Hono, Zod and JOSE Cloudflare Worker API for validation, rate limiting, notification queues, audit-safe errors and sensitive mutations.
Integrated Firebase Authentication, Firestore real-time listeners, Cloud Messaging, App Check and Crashlytics across the system.
Implemented short-lived signed Cloudinary uploads for report media and chat attachments while retaining compatibility with legacy URL-only records.
Created security rules, additive migration tools and automated Worker, web, Android and Firestore-rule tests.
features: Email/password and Google authentication with password recovery
Android and responsive web clients sharing live data
Lost/found reports with signed images, search and filters
Real-time inbox, unread state and media attachments
Blocking, abuse reporting and privacy-limited moderation
Push-notification preferences and private message previews
Matched, resolved and reopened report lifecycle
Queued account deletion and history anonymisation
Light, dark and system appearance modes

challenges.title: Real-time reads with trusted writes
challenges.description: Firestore listeners preserve immediate cross-client updates, while business mutations pass through the Worker so claim races, suspensions, blocks, notifications and audit errors follow one policy.

challenges.title: Compatibility without destructive migration
challenges.description: Additive schemas and fallback reads preserve existing users, URL-only images, reports and conversations while new records gain structured assets, claims and moderation metadata.

challenges.title: Production behavior on free infrastructure
challenges.description: The backend combines Firebase Spark, Cloudflare Workers and Queues, and Cloudinary signed media while surfacing quota or connectivity failures as actionable states instead of false empty screens.

A two-account acceptance run created four meaningful reports, matched reciprocal claims and exchanged three-message private handover conversations through the live web client backed by the same Firebase project used by Android.
